body.hook: Drumlines, hip-hop beats and body-percussion groups like STOMP all start with the same idea: a short rhythm that repeats. Today you become the composer and write a four-bar rhythm of your own.

study.title: Compose a Beat
study.question: How do I compose and notate a rhythm?
study.passage:
Composition steps (written for this lesson):
1. Explore (5 minutes): Try four body-percussion sounds: stomp (low), pat thighs (medium), clap (high), snap (very high).
2. Motif (5 minutes): Create a one-bar idea using quarter and eighth notes.
3. Build four bars (10 minutes): A common shape is A A B A: bar 1 = motif, bar 2 = repeat, bar 3 = something new, bar 4 = motif again or a strong ending. Include at least one rest.
4. Notate (10 minutes): Write it in 4/4 with bar lines, and add which body sound plays each note (S, P, C or Sn) under the notes. Check each bar adds to 4 beats.
5. Perform (10 minutes): Perform it four times in a row with a steady beat. A partner checks it matches the notation.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Perform it four times with a steady beat
discussion: Why does A A B A work well?
Did every bar add up to 4 beats?
Did your performance match your notation?
study.product: Notate and perform an original four-bar rhythm in 4/4 with body percussion, labelled with sounds and counts.

body.objective: Students will be able to layer rhythms into a group piece.
body.iCan: I can layer rhythms into a group piece.
successCriteria: I can layer rhythms to create a group piece
I can hold my part while others play different rhythms
I can use dynamics and entrances to shape a piece
body.hook: One rhythm alone is a pattern. Stack four different rhythms on top of each other and it becomes a groove. This is how drum circles, samba bands and electronic music producers build exciting music.

study.title: Build the Groove
study.question: How do layered rhythms create a group piece?
study.passage:
Group composition (written for this lesson):
Groups of four combine their four-bar rhythms from last lesson.
1. Choose roles (5 minutes): Part 1 = low, steady pulse (the heartbeat, often stomps on beats 1 and 3); Part 2 = medium ostinato; Part 3 = high, busier rhythm; Part 4 = the "solo" with the most interesting rhythm.
2. Structure (10 minutes): Plan entrances: bars 1–4 Part 1 alone; bars 5–8 add Part 2; bars 9–12 add Part 3; bars 13–16 add Part 4; bars 17–20 everyone, then a big ending on a cue.
3. Dynamics (5 minutes): Start piano and crescendo as layers enter; finish forte.
4. Rehearse (15 minutes): One person counts in "1, 2, 3, 4." Practise holding your part while others play.
5. Score (5 minutes): Write a simple chart showing which parts play in each section.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to perform and reflect.
successCriteria: I can perform my group piece with a steady beat and dynamics
I can reflect on a performance using musical vocabulary

body.hook: Professional musicians record their performances, listen back and make notes. What sounded perfect while playing often sounds different on the recording. Today you perform your group piece and reflect like a professional.

vocabulary.definition: Thinking about and evaluating your work.
How well the parts can be heard in relation to each other.

study.title: Perform and Reflect
study.question: How do musicians evaluate and improve a performance?
study.passage:
Performance plan (written for this lesson):
1. Warm-up (5 minutes): Clap the pulse together; run each layer once.
2. Performance (15 minutes): Each group performs its piece for the class; the teacher records it on a tablet if possible.
3. Peer feedback (10 minutes): For each group, two listeners give one glow and one grow using criteria: steady tempo, accurate rhythms, clear entrances, dynamics, balance, ending together.
4. Listen back (10 minutes): Groups watch or listen to their recording.
5. Reflection (10 minutes): Each student rates the group 1–4 on each criterion and writes: one thing that went well, one thing to improve, and what you learned about composing.
Audience etiquette: stay quiet during performances, applaud at the end and give specific, kind feedback.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Give and receive glow and grow feedback
discussion: Did the tempo stay steady? How do you know?
What did the recording reveal that you didn't notice while playing?
What would you change in your composition?
study.product: Perform your group piece and write a reflection rating six criteria with evidence and one next step.
